strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual framing: reframing SAM/SAM2 adaptation for prompt-absent tasks as a prompt-space conditioning problem rather than feature-space patching is a reasonably novel perspective that is distinct from prior adapter-based COD approaches.

Extensive and well-organized ablation studies (Tables 2 and 3) that isolate the contributions of SPG, PSG, lateral regularization, refinement head, LoRA placement, and specific design choices within PSG (asymmetric gating vs. subtraction/concatenation/cross-attention, residual anchoring point), providing good evidence that each component contributes meaningfully.

Strong quantitative results across four COD benchmarks under a controlled, deterministic no-external-prompt protocol, with all baselines re-trained under identical conditions for fairness, which strengthens the validity of the comparisons.

Demonstration of cross-domain generalization to medical polyp segmentation (zero-shot transfer from Kvasir-SEG to CVC-ClinicDB and ETIS) supports the claim that the proposed conditioning paradigm is not narrowly overfit to COD.
Useful qualitative and internal feature visualizations (Fig. 4) that meaningfully illustrate how PSG suppresses background activations, aiding interpretability of the proposed gating mechanism.
Reasonable parameter efficiency (21.26M trainable parameters) relative to full fine-tuning and several specialist baselines, with reported multi-seed stability (MAE 0.017 ± 0.001).
weaknesses: The method's effectiveness appears strongly tied to the scale of the underlying foundation model backbone (SAM2-L); performance collapses substantially for SAM2-T/B, which raises questions about the generality/practicality of the approach outside large-backbone regimes, and this limitation is only briefly acknowledged.

The full fine-tuning variant (SAM2-L, FT) with far more trainable parameters (231.86M) underperforms the LoRA r32 variant (21.26M) on several metrics; this counterintuitive result is not sufficiently analyzed or explained, leaving open questions about training stability, overfitting, or optimization confounds.

Comparisons against very recent prompt-free/self-prompting SAM baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., hierarchical self-prompting SAM, test-time calibration methods) are largely qualitative/discussed rather than benchmarked quantitatively, weakening the completeness of the empirical comparison against the most relevant competing paradigm.

Training details (single RTX 3090, batch size 1, 100 epochs) suggest limited-scale experiments; it is unclear whether baseline methods were tuned to their optimal hyperparameters under this constrained setup or simply run with default settings, which could bias comparisons.

No mention of code, model, or data release, which combined with the architectural complexity (multiple custom modules, specific hyperparameters for conv/gating blocks) raises reproducibility concerns.

The theoretical justification for why prompt-space conditioning is fundamentally superior to feature-space adaptation is largely argued qualitatively/rhetorically (e.g., "weakly activated pathway") rather than through a more rigorous mechanistic or theoretical analysis, and the empirical support (FeatAdd ablation) is relatively narrow (one alternative fusion baseline).

The Oracle comparison (1-point GT prompt) as a benchmark for "native capacity" is somewhat unconventional and may not be the most rigorous way to contextualize gains, since a single point is a weak/ambiguous prompt for camouflaged targets by design, making the comparison less informative than it might first appear.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated structural problem: SAM/SAM2's decoder is inherently prompt-conditioned, yet many deployment scenarios (e.g., camouflaged object detection) require fully automatic, prompt-absent inference. Framing prior feature-space adaptation methods as bypassing the native prompt interface is a useful and novel conceptual framing.

The core technical idea -- synthesizing intrinsic dense/sparse prompts (SPG) and routing them through SAM2's frozen prompt encoder to reactivate native prompt-conditioned decoding, rather than injecting signals into intermediate features -- is a reasonably original contribution distinct from prior self-prompting or feature-adapter approaches.

Prompt-Space Gating (PSG) is a sensible mechanism for camouflage-specific foreground/background disambiguation, and the design choice of anchoring the residual to the unsuppressed Z+ rather than the suppressed feature is well-motivated and empirically validated.

Extensive and well-structured ablations (Tables 2 and 3) systematically isolate the contributions of SPG, PSG, lateral regularization, refinement head, LoRA placement, and internal PSG design choices (fusion operator, residual anchoring, token replacement), which supports the soundness of the architectural claims.

Strong quantitative results across four standard COD benchmarks against both specialist models and SAM/SAM2 adaptation baselines, all retrained under a controlled, identical prompt-absent protocol for fairness, with reported multi-seed stability (MAE 0.017 ± 0.001).

Demonstration of cross-domain generalization to medical polyp segmentation (zero-shot transfer from Kvasir-SEG to CVC-ClinicDB/ETIS) strengthens the claim that the proposed conditioning paradigm is not COD-specific.

Good interpretability effort via internal feature visualizations (Fig. 4) showing the gate decision map and feature energy changes, which helps substantiate the claimed mechanism of action rather than treating PSG as a black box.
Efficient adaptation footprint (21.26M trainable parameters, frozen prompt encoder and image encoder aside from LoRA) is a meaningful practical advantage over full fine-tuning or heavier adapters.
weaknesses: The main state-of-the-art comparison table omits several recent SAM-based COD methods explicitly discussed in the related work section (e.g., SAM-COD+, dual-stream SAM adapters, SAM2-DFBCNet), leaving the state-of-the-art claim less fully substantiated than it could be.

An unexplained inconsistency exists between the full fine-tuning variant (IP-SAM SAM2-L, FT, 231.86M trainable params) and the LoRA r32 variant (21.26M params): the far more heavily tuned FT model actually underperforms the lightweight LoRA variant on MAE for CAMO (0.040 vs 0.032) and COD10K (0.018 vs 0.017). This counterintuitive result is not discussed or analyzed, which weakens confidence in the interpretation of parameter efficiency versus adaptation capacity.

Effectiveness is closely tied to the scale of the underlying foundation model; performance drops substantially on smaller SAM2 variants (T/B), which somewhat undercuts the generality of the proposed paradigm outside of large-capacity backbones, though this is acknowledged as a limitation.

Training uses batch size 1 on a single RTX 3090 for all methods; while this ensures fairness, it raises questions about whether reported gaps would hold under more standard training regimes with larger batch sizes, and no discussion of this choice's impact is provided.

The medical polyp cross-dataset results, while generally favorable, are not uniformly best (e.g., LACFormer achieves higher mIoU on ETIS), so the abstract's characterization of 'strong zero-shot transfer' is somewhat optimistic relative to the more mixed quantitative picture in Table 4.

The comparison against a SAM2 'Oracle' prompted with a ground-truth centroid point is interesting but not entirely apples-to-apples, since the Oracle lacks any task-specific training/adaptation; presenting this as evidence that IP-SAM exceeds the model's 'native capacity' could be read as somewhat overstated.

The manuscript's prose is heavy with repeated rhetorical framing (e.g., 'structural paradox,' 'native manifold') across the introduction, related work, and method sections, which adds length without proportional new information and could be tightened.
No FLOPs, memory, or wall-clock training time comparisons are reported beyond FPS at inference and parameter counts, limiting a full picture of practical adaptation cost relative to baselines.

strengths: Addresses a clearly articulated and practically relevant problem: the structural mismatch between prompt-conditioned decoders (SAM/SAM2) and prompt-absent automatic deployment, which is well-motivated for camouflaged object detection (COD) and beyond.

The core method (SPG generating intrinsic dense/sparse prompts routed through the frozen prompt encoder, plus PSG's asymmetric suppressive gating) is technically clear and clearly diagrammed (Figs. 1-2), with an explicit, well-justified mechanism (anchoring residual to unsuppressed Z+ rather than the suppressed feature) supported by ablations.

Extensive empirical validation: SOTA results across 4 COD benchmarks under a consistent, deterministic no-external-prompt protocol, with all baselines re-trained under identical conditions for fairness; results reported with multi-seed variance on the main table.

Very thorough ablation studies (Tables 2, 3, 6) that carefully decouple the source of performance gains, e.g., showing that routing through the frozen prompt encoder—rather than merely having a stronger decoder or bypassing the encoder—drives the improvement, and that raw continuous logits outperform binarized/sigmoid/scaled variants.

Strong generalization evidence: cross-dataset transfer to medical polyp segmentation (Table 4) and an appendix study on five standard SOD benchmarks (Table 5) using the identical architecture/recipe, supporting the claim that the paradigm is not COD-specific.

Includes a transparent computational efficiency breakdown (wall-clock and CUDA-synchronized component profiling) showing modest overhead (~20.7% latency increase, with the added modules contributing only ~13% of internal compute).

Commendably honest and mechanistic failure-mode analysis (Section G) that visualizes and explains under-segmentation failures caused by negative-prompt encroachment, rather than merely asserting limitations qualitatively.
weaknesses: The absolute improvement over the strongest SAM-based baseline (SAM2-Adapter, SAM2-L r80, which also fine-tunes with LoRA) is often modest (e.g., Sm 0.912 vs 0.900 on CAMO, 0.911 vs 0.904 on NC4K), which somewhat tempers the 'substantially superior disambiguation' framing in the text.

The conceptual novelty is incremental relative to prior self-prompting/automatic-prompting SAM adaptation literature (acknowledged related works generate dense conceptual prompts); the main differentiator (asymmetric background gating and frozen-encoder routing) is a reasonable but modest architectural innovation rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

Training setup is limited (single RTX 3090, batch size 1, 100 epochs), and most ablation/variant tables (2, 3, 6) report single-run numbers without variance, unlike the main results table, making some fine-grained comparisons (e.g., differences of 0.001-0.002 MAE) less statistically convincing.

The method introduces considerable architectural complexity (dual-branch SPG, PSG with multiple sub-blocks, optional lateral/refinement heads, several loss weighting terms), which increases the risk of overfitting to the specific benchmark setup and makes reproducibility more demanding despite the parameter count being modest.

The comparison against the 'Oracle' (ground-truth centroid point) SAM2 baseline, while interesting, is somewhat apples-to-oranges since the Oracle lacks any task-specific adaptation, so the framing of IP-SAM 'outperforming' it should be read cautiously (which the authors do partially acknowledge).

Some terminology proliferation (prompt-space conditioning, intrinsic prompts, prompt-space gating, prompt manifold) adds rhetorical weight but occasionally obscures a comparatively straightforward technical contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated structural problem: prompt-conditioned segmenters (SAM/SAM2) are designed around explicit spatial prompts, yet many practical deployments require fully automatic segmentation; the paper frames this mismatch precisely and proposes a principled solution.

The core idea of prompt-space conditioning (synthesizing dense/sparse intrinsic prompts and routing them through the frozen prompt encoder rather than only injecting into intermediate features) is conceptually clean and, importantly, is validated through a carefully decoupled ablation (Table 6 in appendix / 'Bypass Prompt Encoder' vs 'Prompt-Space Cond.') that isolates the effect of routing through the native prompt manifold from mere decoder redesign or additional parameters.

Prompt-Space Gating (PSG) is a sensible, well-motivated mechanism for camouflage/low-contrast domains, and the anchored-residual design choice is empirically justified against several alternatives (subtraction, concatenation, cross-attention fusion, anchoring to suppressed feature).

Extensive experimental validation: 4 COD benchmarks with SOTA results at only 21.26M trainable parameters, plus appendix experiments on 5 SOD benchmarks and cross-dataset medical polyp segmentation, showing the approach is not narrowly overfit to one task.

Thorough ablation studies covering component contributions (SPG/PSG/Lateral/Refine), input logit formats for the prompt encoder, LoRA injection strategies, and PSG operator choices, which collectively strengthen the causal story behind the method's gains.
Reasonably transparent efficiency analysis (wall-clock and CUDA-synchronized component profiling) showing modest overhead (~20.7%) relative to the base SAM2 model.

Honest and detailed failure-mode analysis (Appendix G) that mechanistically explains under-segmentation failures via negative-prompt encroachment, which adds credibility and clarifies the operating boundary of the method rather than overclaiming robustness.
weaknesses: Performance degrades substantially when using smaller SAM2 backbones (SAM2-T/B), with MAE increasing by roughly 3-5x relative to SAM2-L; this raises questions about whether the core contribution (prompt-space conditioning) is fundamentally dependent on a very large, high-capacity frozen backbone rather than being a generally applicable adaptation strategy.

There appears to be a numbering inconsistency between the main text (which refers to 'Tab. 6' when discussing conditioning paradigm and SPG capacity ablations) and the actual table numbering in the provided manuscript (Table 3), suggesting either a mismatch in cross-referencing or a discrepancy between the main paper and appendix table numbering that should be corrected.

Training is conducted with batch size 1 on a single RTX 3090 across all baselines; while this supports fairness of comparison, it leaves some uncertainty about how results would generalize under more standard multi-GPU/larger-batch training regimes typical of foundation-model fine-tuning literature.

While the appendix reports 3-seed averaging on the main COD results, most ablation and appendix tables (SOD, medical, decoupling studies) do not report variance across seeds, which somewhat limits certainty about the significance of some fine-grained comparisons (e.g., 0.001-0.002 MAE differences between closely competing ablation variants).

The novelty of using self-generated dense/sparse prompts is incremental relative to existing self-prompting and automatic-prompting literature (e.g., prior dense conceptual prompt generation methods cited in Related Work); the primary differentiator is the asymmetric PSG gating and strict routing through the frozen encoder, which, while empirically supported, is a comparatively narrow methodological novelty.
